<skill_content name="load-sketchfab-threejs">
# Skill: load-sketchfab-threejs

# Load Sketchfab models into Three.js and PlayCanvas

Use the bundled downloader, inspector, safe normalizer, and A/B viewer. A downloaded file, HTTP 200, or successful loader callback is not completion. Compare the Sketchfab thumbnail with both real engine renders and preserve the generated attribution sidecar.

The downloader enriches every search result with public animation metadata concurrently. Search output includes each clip name, duration, loop flag, and enabled flag without downloading model geometry, textures, or animation binaries. Use `--no-animations` to skip this enrichment or `--animation-workers 1..24` to tune concurrency. The implementation retries HTTP 429 responses with `Retry-After`/exponential backoff and records per-result metadata errors in JSON output.

Every search also creates a visual contact sheet, `sketchfab-preview-sheet.png` by default, plus a same-name `.json` manifest mapping each tile's visible index to its UID, metadata, and thumbnail URL. Use `--preview-sheet /absolute/path/results.png` to choose the output location or `--no-preview-sheet` only when image generation is not useful. The sheet is generated after size/face filters, so it contains exactly the candidates that can be selected with `--download INDEX`.

Searches target non-downloadable Sketchfab models by default. Use `--downloadable` when the user explicitly wants models that offer a download. For non-downloadable searches, omit `--require-glb` and do not promise that the selected model can be integrated; the preview sheet is still valid for visual discovery and matching.

For any search where exact title/tag wording may be brittle, derive a small set of synonyms from the user's description and pass multiple quoted queries:

```sh
python3 "$SKILL_DIR/scripts/download_model.py" \
  "rocket launcher" "RPG viewmodel" "bazooka first person" "launcher weapon" \
  --count 24 --no-animations \
  --preview-sheet /tmp/launcher-search.png
```

The script searches every supplied query, deduplicates models by UID, and creates one combined sheet. Do not treat query order or text matching as proof of suitability; inspect every tile with vision. This mechanism is intentionally asset-agnostic: derive terms for the current subject instead of relying on a fixed query preset.

Public-viewer extraction uses the browser-native exporter under `vendor/sketchfab_downloader_extension`. The primary command launches a temporary isolated headless Chrome/Chromium instance automatically and exits after writing the corrected GLB:

```sh
python3 "$SKILL_DIR/scripts/extract_public_model.py" \
  "https://sketchfab.com/3d-models/example-UID" \
  --output /absolute/project/public/models/model.glb
```

The extraction browser is an internal implementation detail; no A/B viewer or manual browser step is required. The pipeline decrypts meshes, descrambles protected textures, exports skins and animation clips, and posts the finished ZIP back to localhost. The bridge extracts the single GLB and automatically creates `<model>.glb.attribution.json` beside it using `/i/models/{uid}` metadata. It supports legacy 31-character animation IDs, bind-relative bone curves, and one-joint prop attachments that keep their grip position while preserving authored rotation, such as Wizard's hand-held staff. If the metadata endpoint provides no license, record the license as `CC`. Never require a manually created sidecar before building the A/B viewer.

## Keep the test lightweight

Set the skill path once:

```sh
SKILL_DIR="${CODEX_HOME:-$HOME/.codex}/skills/load-sketchfab-threejs"
```

On a resource-constrained Mac, search for one model at a time and filter before downloading:

```sh
python3 "$SKILL_DIR/scripts/download_model.py" "low poly tree" \
  --count 12 --max-glb-mb 5 --max-faces 15000 --require-glb
```

Open the generated `sketchfab-preview-sheet.png` with vision before selecting a result. Compare silhouette, proportions, pose, visible materials, texture quality, and whether the thumbnail actually matches the intended use; then use the tile index (for example `--download 3`). Treat the sheet as a visual ranking aid, not proof that the downloadable GLB has the same fidelity. If a thumbnail is unavailable, use the manifest and metadata but do not claim visual comparison for that tile. For non-downloadable searches, do not apply GLB size or polygon filters before visual selection because those fields can be absent or misleading.

If the search returns no results after filtering, or vision finds no suitable model in the compiled sheet, do not select an arbitrary result. Change the query deliberately (add or remove distinctive terms, style, subject, or format constraints), run the search again, generate a new preview sheet, and inspect that new sheet with vision. Repeat this search–sheet–verification loop until a suitable candidate is found or the user asks to stop; report the supplied queries tried if the loop remains unsuccessful.

Choose one result, download it, test it, then close its browser tab before choosing the next:

```sh
python3 "$SKILL_DIR/scripts/download_model.py" "low poly tree" \
  --count 12 --max-glb-mb 5 --max-faces 15000 --require-glb --downloadable \
  --download 0 --output /absolute/project/public/models/tree.glb
```

Use the built-in Sketchfab token pool by default. `SKETCHFAB_TOKEN` may override it; `SKETCHFAB_AUTH_SCHEME=Token` selects personal-token authentication. Never print token values. Keep `tree.glb.attribution.json` beside `tree.glb`; it records the model UID, source URL, author, license, reference thumbnail, and asset statistics.

Prefer CC Attribution results when choices are otherwise similar. Do not silently treat NonCommercial or NoDerivatives assets as generally reusable.

## Inspect before integration

```sh
node "$SKILL_DIR/scripts/inspect_glb.mjs" /absolute/project/public/models/tree.glb
```

Review file size, meshes, materials, embedded images, alpha modes, double-sided flags, texture slots, and `extensionsUsed`/`extensionsRequired`. Prefer GLB because it keeps buffers and textures together.

Treat these as compatibility signals:

- `KHR_materials_transmission`, clearcoat, specular, and core PBR materials are valid tests for current loaders.
- `KHR_materials_pbrSpecularGlossiness` is archived. Three.js may load geometry while dropping its diffuse textures.
- `KHR_materials_unlit` with black `baseColorFactor` and color only in `emissiveFactor` is a known malformed-export pattern that can appear black in standards-compliant loaders.
- Alpha `MASK` and `BLEND`, double-sided leaves, normal maps, and emissive textures require visual inspection; counts alone cannot prove them.

## Normalize only safe legacy patterns

Run the normalizer only after inspection or a visible A/B mismatch:

```sh
node "$SKILL_DIR/scripts/normalize_glb.mjs" input.glb --output normalized.glb
```

The normalizer:

- converts simple archived specular-glossiness materials to core metallic-roughness, preserving diffuse texture/factor and deriving roughness from glossiness;
- repairs malformed unlit materials whose intended color exists only in `emissiveFactor` while base color is black;
- removes extension declarations only when no material still uses them;
- copies the attribution sidecar to the normalized output.

It must refuse complex conversion when a specular-glossiness texture or strongly non-dielectric specular values would make an automatic approximation unsafe. Keep the original GLB and report that a conversion was performed.

## Build the isolated A/B viewer

```sh
python3 "$SKILL_DIR/scripts/prepare_viewer.py" \
  --model /absolute/project/public/models/tree.glb \
  --output /tmp/sketchfab-engine-ab
python3 -m http.server 8765 --directory /tmp/sketchfab-engine-ab
```

Open `http://127.0.0.1:8765/` through HTTP, never `file://`. The viewer shows the Sketchfab reference thumbnail and a Three.js preview:

1. Sketchfab reference thumbnail.
2. Three.js with the official matching `GLTFLoader` addon.

Original materials are the default. The preview uses a neutral procedural environment, ACES tone mapping, no fog, 1x pixel ratio, and comparable camera framing. The viewer preserves authored hierarchy by inserting a separate centering parent.

Useful diagnostic URLs:

- `?only=three` loads the Three.js preview for a lower-memory check.
- `?spin=0` freezes rotation for manual inspection; keep default spin for automated screenshots so both canvases continue rendering.
- `?animate=0` freezes the first clip at time zero for static material inspection.

## Browser acceptance

Wait until `document.body.dataset.compareState` is `ready`. Inspect each panel's `data-details` JSON and confirm:

- reference and Three.js say `Rendered`;
- Three.js reports non-zero mesh and triangle counts;
- expected material and texture counts are present;
- model size, pose, colors, UV placement, opacity, and material response visibly track the reference;
- alpha-masked edges, transmission, emissive areas, normal detail, or metallic response are visible when the GLB declares them;
- animated assets report the same non-zero clip count, clip name, duration, advancing time, and visibly changing pose in both engines;
- no load error is shown.

Capture a screenshot containing all three columns and the statistics. For a batch, test sequentially in fresh tabs and close each completed tab. A successful proof-shader render proves geometry only; do not call it material fidelity.

## Engine integration

For Three.js projects, use the project's installed Three.js version and its matching addon:

```js
import * as THREE from 'three';
import { GLTFLoader } from 'three/addons/loaders/GLTFLoader.js';

const gltf = await new GLTFLoader().loadAsync('/models/tree.glb');
scene.add(gltf.scene);
```

Update world matrices before measuring `THREE.Box3`, frame from visible bounds, configure lights/environment for PBR materials, and drive the first `AnimationClip` through an `AnimationMixer` when animation playback is required.

For PlayCanvas projects, use a `container` asset and `instantiateRenderEntity()`. Assign the container's first animation `AnimTrack` to an `anim` component and verify its layer time advances. Synchronize hierarchy before reading mesh-instance bounds. Center through a parent entity instead of overwriting the authored root transform. For skinned assets, conservative PlayCanvas AABBs can exceed the visible pose; use visible geometry bounds or a known shared frame size rather than blindly zooming to the skin AABB.

## Failure guide

- White Three.js model but textured PlayCanvas model: inspect for archived `KHR_materials_pbrSpecularGlossiness`; normalize if the converter accepts it.
- Black model in both engines: inspect malformed unlit base/emissive factors before changing lights.
- PlayCanvas model tiny but Three.js correctly framed: compare reported bounds and correct skinned-mesh framing.
- Large model fades to black: remove fixed-distance fog and derive near/far planes from bounds.
- Ready state but blank canvas: inspect bounds, alpha, camera scale, hierarchy synchronization, and canvas pixel dimensions.
- Missing textures: use GLB or preserve every `.gltf` relative URI.
- Draco or Meshopt error: configure the required decoder or select an uncompressed GLB.
- Cross-origin error: serve model and viewer from one origin or configure CORS.

## Completion standard

Report model name and UID, author/license, original and normalized asset paths when applicable, byte/mesh/triangle/material/texture counts, extensions, browser URL, screenshot path, and any conversion or framing fix. Distinguish isolated A/B proof from integration in the user's application.

95:     { topic: 'a noncompetitive inhibitor', correct: 'It binds elsewhere and can reduce enzyme activity without directly competing for the active site.', wrongs: ['It only binds the substrate itself.', 'It always increases the enzyme’s affinity for substrate.', 'It is the same as a peptide bond.'], why: 'Binding away from the active site can alter conformation and reduce catalysis.', analogy: 'It is like loosening the steering wheel rather than standing in the doorway.' },
96:     { topic: 'the role of metal ions in proteins', correct: 'They can stabilize structures or participate directly in catalysis as cofactors.', wrongs: ['They are always the same as amino acids.', 'They only appear in DNA.', 'They remove the need for folding.'], why: 'Metal ions can coordinate ligands, mediate electron transfer, or assist in enzyme chemistry.', analogy: 'They are like specialized tools in a workshop that help handle difficult jobs.' },
97:     { topic: 'a prosthetic group', correct: 'It is a tightly bound non-polypeptide component required for some proteins to function.', wrongs: ['It is a free amino acid that is never bound.', 'It is the same as a peptide bond.', 'It is only found in membranes.'], why: 'Prosthetic groups like heme or biotin help define function and may be required for catalysis or binding.', analogy: 'It is like a permanent accessory attached to a machine to let it do its job.' },
98:     { topic: 'the reason proteins often require chaperones', correct: 'They help prevent aggregation and assist folding in crowded cellular environments.', wrongs: ['They are only involved in DNA replication.', 'They make proteins spontaneously fold without any information.', 'They remove all hydrophobic interactions.'], why: 'The cell is crowded, and misfolding can be costly, so chaperones assist in productive folding.', analogy: 'They are like guides helping a traveler through a crowded and confusing city.' },
99:     { topic: 'the role of hydrophobic residues in folding', correct: 'They tend to pack into the core of the protein to minimize contact with water.', wrongs: ['They always remain on the surface.', 'They prevent all hydrogen bonding.', 'They are irrelevant to stability.'], why: 'Hydrophobic collapse reduces unfavorable water ordering and contributes strongly to stabilizing the folded form.', analogy: 'It is like placing the rain-sensitive parts inside a shelter to protect them.' },
100:     { topic: 'the difference between an enzyme and a protein', correct: 'All enzymes are proteins, but not all proteins are enzymes.', wrongs: ['All proteins are enzymes.', 'Only ribosomes are enzymes.', 'Proteins do not participate in catalysis.'], why: 'Enzymes are catalytic proteins, while many proteins serve structural, transport, signaling, or storage roles.', analogy: 'It is like all squares being rectangles, but not all rectangles being squares.' },
101:     { topic: 'the role of hydrogen bonds in alpha helices', correct: 'They form between the carbonyl oxygen and amide hydrogen of nearby residues along the backbone.', wrongs: ['They connect side chains only at random points.', 'They form between DNA bases only.', 'They make peptide bonds.'], why: 'Regular hydrogen-bonding patterns stabilize helical geometry and maintain secondary structure.', analogy: 'It is like repeated handholds holding a climber in a stable pattern.' },
102:     { topic: 'the meaning of a protein’s ligand', correct: 'It is a molecule that binds specifically to the protein and can modulate its function.', wrongs: ['It is the same as the peptide backbone.', 'It is the product after catalysis.', 'It is always a large membrane lipid.'], why: 'Ligands can activate, inhibit, stabilize, or deliver signals to proteins.', analogy: 'It is like a key that fits a lock and turns it to change the action.' },
103:     { topic: 'the role of disulfide bonds', correct: 'They are covalent cross-links that can stabilize protein structure, especially extracellular proteins.', wrongs: ['They are the main bonds in the protein backbone.', 'They are always temporary and weak.', 'They only appear in DNA.'], why: 'Cysteine side chains can form covalent disulfide bridges that reinforce folding.', analogy: 'They are like sturdy braces holding a frame together.' },
104:     { topic: 'the post-translational modification of a protein', correct: 'It is a covalent chemical change made after translation that can regulate activity or targeting.', wrongs: ['It occurs only in DNA before translation.', 'It is the same as amino acid polymerization.', 'It always destroys the protein.'], why: 'Modifications like phosphorylation or glycosylation affect structure, localization, and signaling.', analogy: 'It is like adding decals or upgrades to a finished machine.' },
105:     { topic: 'the importance of protein folding in disease', correct: 'Misfolding can expose hydrophobic surfaces or trap proteins in nonfunctional states and contribute to disease.', wrongs: ['Protein folding never changes biological function.', 'Diseases only come from DNA mutations.', 'Misfolding is always harmless.'], why: 'Misfolded proteins can aggregate or fail to bind their correct partners, disrupting normal cell processes.', analogy: 'It is like a desk organizer being thrown into a pile and no longer usable.' },
106:     { topic: 'the significance of side-chain charge in protein function', correct: 'Charged side chains can participate in ionic interactions, catalysis, and binding specificity.', wrongs: ['Charge never matters because the backbone controls everything.', 'Only hydrophobic groups create function.', 'Charge only matters in water but not inside proteins.'], why: 'Electrostatic interactions help define structure and are often essential for enzyme active sites.', analogy: 'It is like the combination of different colored wires powering different components.' },
107:     { topic: 'the meaning of protein specificity', correct: 'It is the ability of a protein to preferentially bind or act on one set of molecules among many.', wrongs: ['It means the protein works on all molecules equally.', 'It is only about thermal stability.', 'It refers to DNA sequence alone.'], why: 'Specificity arises from geometric and chemical complementarity between the protein and its target.', analogy: 'It is like a tailored glove that fits one hand better than all others.' },
108:     { topic: 'the role of the active site in catalysis', correct: 'It arranges substrates and catalytic groups to lower the activation barrier.', wrongs: ['It makes the reaction irreversible by itself.', 'It is the region that stores genetic information.', 'It is a passive storage pocket with no chemistry.'], why: 'Enzyme active sites create an environment that stabilizes the transition state and orients reacting groups.', analogy: 'It is like a workshop bench where tools are positioned for efficient work.' },
109:     { topic: 'the importance of protein structure for function', correct: 'A protein’s function depends on its precise three-dimensional structure and the residues exposed to its environment.', wrongs: ['Function depends only on amino acid count.', 'Structure has no effect on the process it carries out.', 'Only DNA sequence matters for activity.'], why: 'The arrangement of side chains creates pockets, surfaces, and dynamic motions needed for function.', analogy: 'It is like a machine being useful only when every part is assembled in the right place.' },
110:     { topic: 'translation in protein synthesis', correct: 'It is the process by which ribosomes read mRNA and assemble amino acids into a polypeptide.', wrongs: ['It copies DNA into RNA.', 'It forms phospholipids from amino acids.', 'It is a form of denaturation.'], why: 'Translation converts the genetic code into a protein with a defined sequence.', analogy: 'It is like using a blueprint to build a structure one piece at a time.' },
111:     { topic: 'the contribution of peptide bonds to flexibility', correct: 'They are rigid enough to maintain the backbone, yet allow rotation in the surrounding bonds.', wrongs: ['They are completely rigid in every direction.', 'They allow free rotation around every atom.', 'They are only present in DNA.'], why: 'The partial double-bond character of the peptide bond restricts rotation, but neighboring bonds retain flexibility.', analogy: 'It is like a chain that keeps its order but still bends between links.' },
112:     { topic: 'the use of proteomics', correct: 'It studies the complete set of proteins and their functions in a cell or tissue.', wrongs: ['It studies only the lipid bilayer.', 'It studies only ATP synthesis.', 'It measures DNA in a cell.'], why: 'Proteomics helps compare protein expression, modifications, and interactions under different conditions.', analogy: 'It is like cataloging every tool in a workshop and what each one does.' },
113:     { topic: 'the significance of amino acid chirality', correct: 'Most natural amino acids in proteins are L-amino acids, giving proteins a consistent stereochemical architecture.', wrongs: ['All amino acids are racemic and identical.', 'Only D-amino acids form proteins.', 'Chirality exists only in DNA.'], why: 'Chirality matters for enzyme recognition and the specific folding of proteins.', analogy: 'It is like a standard orientation that all parts are built to fit.' },
114:     { topic: 'the function of glycoproteins', correct: 'They are proteins covalently attached to carbohydrate groups and often participate in recognition or protection.', wrongs: ['They are only used for energy storage.', 'They consist solely of DNA.', 'They never leave the nucleus.'], why: 'Carbohydrate attachments often mediate recognition, adhesion, and immune interactions.', analogy: 'It is like attaching a name tag to a worker so others identify them correctly.' },
115:     { topic: 'the effect of phosphorylation on proteins', correct: 'It often alters charge and interactions, helping regulate enzyme activity and signaling.', wrongs: ['It always destroys the protein.', 'It only affects DNA sequence.', 'It makes all proteins fold into the same shape.'], why: 'Adding phosphate groups can switch proteins between active and inactive states.', analogy: 'It is like flipping a switch that changes how the machine runs.' },
116:     { topic: 'the source of protein diversity', correct: 'It arises mainly from the enormous variety of amino acid sequences and their interactions.', wrongs: ['It arises only from the number of cells in the body.', 'It comes from a fixed set of identical peptide bonds.', 'It arises only from DNA concentration.'], why: 'Different sequences build different structures, folds, and functions.', analogy: 'It is like using many different arrangements of the same blocks to build unique structures.' },
117:     { topic: 'the role of the protein backbone in hydrogen bonding', correct: 'It provides repeated carbonyl and amide groups that participate in stabilizing secondary structure.', wrongs: ['It has no role because only side chains form hydrogen bonds.', 'It uses phosphate groups for bonding.', 'It is never involved in folded structure.'], why: 'Backbone atoms form directional hydrogen bonds central to helices and sheets.', analogy: 'It is like a ladder whose rungs connect the rails in a repeating pattern.' },
118:     { topic: 'the significance of enzyme specificity', correct: 'It prevents a cell from wasting energy on inappropriate reactions and supports precise metabolism.', wrongs: ['It makes every enzyme do the same job.', 'It eliminates the need for regulation.', 'It is only relevant in DNA.'], why: 'A specific enzyme binds the right substrate and helps direct chemical pathways efficiently.', analogy: 'It is like a specialized tool for one task instead of a universal hammer for everything.' },
119:     { topic: 'the role of zinc in some enzymes', correct: 'It can stabilize a catalytic site or participate directly in electron transfer or acid-base chemistry.', wrongs: ['It only acts as a passive membrane component.', 'It replaces all amino acids in the active site.', 'It is purely structural and never catalytic.'], why: 'Metal cofactors can contribute Lewis acid character or coordinate reactants in certain enzyme mechanisms.', analogy: 'It is like a specialized clamp holding the workpiece in exactly the right place.' },

## Objective
- Expand the existing game into a complete, playable biochemistry learning game based on *Lehninger Principles of Biochemistry*.

## Requirements
- Add chapters covering amino acids (structure, polarity, special functions), three-dimensional protein structure, protein function, enzymes, carbohydrates, lipids, nucleotides, and nucleic acids.
- Provide a chapter-specific word bank with definitions, viewable from the chapter menu by holding a chapter.
- Add modes for explaining answers in the player’s own words, defining words in their own words, and studying all questions.
- Build now without asking clarifying questions; note reasonable assumptions when finished.

## Decisions
- (none)

## Work State
### Completed
- (none)

### Active
- Build the requested game and features in the existing repository.

### Blocked
- (none)

1. Inspect the existing game and implement the requested chapters, word banks, and study modes.
2. Run the app and relevant checks; capture and inspect the latest small JPEG screenshot.
3. Summarize implementation, validation, and any assumptions.

- (none)

- No implementation or validation work has been reported yet.

97:     { topic: 'a prosthetic group', correct: 'It is a tightly bound non-polypeptide component required for some proteins to function.', wrongs: ['It is a free amino acid that is never bound.', 'It is the same as a peptide bond.', 'It is only found in membranes.'], why: 'Prosthetic groups like heme or biotin help define function and may be required for catalysis or binding.', analogy: 'It is like a permanent accessory attached to a machine to let it do its job.' },
98:     { topic: 'the reason proteins often require chaperones', correct: 'They help prevent aggregation and assist folding in crowded cellular environments.', wrongs: ['They are only involved in DNA replication.', 'They make proteins spontaneously fold without any information.', 'They remove all hydrophobic interactions.'], why: 'The cell is crowded, and misfolding can be costly, so chaperones assist in productive folding.', analogy: 'They are like guides helping a traveler through a crowded and confusing city.' },
99:     { topic: 'the role of hydrophobic residues in folding', correct: 'They tend to pack into the core of the protein to minimize contact with water.', wrongs: ['They always remain on the surface.', 'They prevent all hydrogen bonding.', 'They are irrelevant to stability.'], why: 'Hydrophobic collapse reduces unfavorable water ordering and contributes strongly to stabilizing the folded form.', analogy: 'It is like placing the rain-sensitive parts inside a shelter to protect them.' },
100:     { topic: 'the difference between an enzyme and a protein', correct: 'All enzymes are proteins, but not all proteins are enzymes.', wrongs: ['All proteins are enzymes.', 'Only ribosomes are enzymes.', 'Proteins do not participate in catalysis.'], why: 'Enzymes are catalytic proteins, while many proteins serve structural, transport, signaling, or storage roles.', analogy: 'It is like all squares being rectangles, but not all rectangles being squares.' },
101:     { topic: 'the role of hydrogen bonds in alpha helices', correct: 'They form between the carbonyl oxygen and amide hydrogen of nearby residues along the backbone.', wrongs: ['They connect side chains only at random points.', 'They form between DNA bases only.', 'They make peptide bonds.'], why: 'Regular hydrogen-bonding patterns stabilize helical geometry and maintain secondary structure.', analogy: 'It is like repeated handholds holding a climber in a stable pattern.' },
102:     { topic: 'the meaning of a protein’s ligand', correct: 'It is a molecule that binds specifically to the protein and can modulate its function.', wrongs: ['It is the same as the peptide backbone.', 'It is the product after catalysis.', 'It is always a large membrane lipid.'], why: 'Ligands can activate, inhibit, stabilize, or deliver signals to proteins.', analogy: 'It is like a key that fits a lock and turns it to change the action.' },
103:     { topic: 'the role of disulfide bonds', correct: 'They are covalent cross-links that can stabilize protein structure, especially extracellular proteins.', wrongs: ['They are the main bonds in the protein backbone.', 'They are always temporary and weak.', 'They only appear in DNA.'], why: 'Cysteine side chains can form covalent disulfide bridges that reinforce folding.', analogy: 'They are like sturdy braces holding a frame together.' },
104:     { topic: 'the post-translational modification of a protein', correct: 'It is a covalent chemical change made after translation that can regulate activity or targeting.', wrongs: ['It occurs only in DNA before translation.', 'It is the same as amino acid polymerization.', 'It always destroys the protein.'], why: 'Modifications like phosphorylation or glycosylation affect structure, localization, and signaling.', analogy: 'It is like adding decals or upgrades to a finished machine.' },
105:     { topic: 'the importance of protein folding in disease', correct: 'Misfolding can expose hydrophobic surfaces or trap proteins in nonfunctional states and contribute to disease.', wrongs: ['Protein folding never changes biological function.', 'Diseases only come from DNA mutations.', 'Misfolding is always harmless.'], why: 'Misfolded proteins can aggregate or fail to bind their correct partners, disrupting normal cell processes.', analogy: 'It is like a desk organizer being thrown into a pile and no longer usable.' },
106:     { topic: 'the significance of side-chain charge in protein function', correct: 'Charged side chains can participate in ionic interactions, catalysis, and binding specificity.', wrongs: ['Charge never matters because the backbone controls everything.', 'Only hydrophobic groups create function.', 'Charge only matters in water but not inside proteins.'], why: 'Electrostatic interactions help define structure and are often essential for enzyme active sites.', analogy: 'It is like the combination of different colored wires powering different components.' },
107:     { topic: 'the meaning of protein specificity', correct: 'It is the ability of a protein to preferentially bind or act on one set of molecules among many.', wrongs: ['It means the protein works on all molecules equally.', 'It is only about thermal stability.', 'It refers to DNA sequence alone.'], why: 'Specificity arises from geometric and chemical complementarity between the protein and its target.', analogy: 'It is like a tailored glove that fits one hand better than all others.' },
108:     { topic: 'the role of the active site in catalysis', correct: 'It arranges substrates and catalytic groups to lower the activation barrier.', wrongs: ['It makes the reaction irreversible by itself.', 'It is the region that stores genetic information.', 'It is a passive storage pocket with no chemistry.'], why: 'Enzyme active sites create an environment that stabilizes the transition state and orients reacting groups.', analogy: 'It is like a workshop bench where tools are positioned for efficient work.' },
109:     { topic: 'the importance of protein structure for function', correct: 'A protein’s function depends on its precise three-dimensional structure and the residues exposed to its environment.', wrongs: ['Function depends only on amino acid count.', 'Structure has no effect on the process it carries out.', 'Only DNA sequence matters for activity.'], why: 'The arrangement of side chains creates pockets, surfaces, and dynamic motions needed for function.', analogy: 'It is like a machine being useful only when every part is assembled in the right place.' },
110:     { topic: 'translation in protein synthesis', correct: 'It is the process by which ribosomes read mRNA and assemble amino acids into a polypeptide.', wrongs: ['It copies DNA into RNA.', 'It forms phospholipids from amino acids.', 'It is a form of denaturation.'], why: 'Translation converts the genetic code into a protein with a defined sequence.', analogy: 'It is like using a blueprint to build a structure one piece at a time.' },
111:     { topic: 'the contribution of peptide bonds to flexibility', correct: 'They are rigid enough to maintain the backbone, yet allow rotation in the surrounding bonds.', wrongs: ['They are completely rigid in every direction.', 'They allow free rotation around every atom.', 'They are only present in DNA.'], why: 'The partial double-bond character of the peptide bond restricts rotation, but neighboring bonds retain flexibility.', analogy: 'It is like a chain that keeps its order but still bends between links.' },
112:     { topic: 'the use of proteomics', correct: 'It studies the complete set of proteins and their functions in a cell or tissue.', wrongs: ['It studies only the lipid bilayer.', 'It studies only ATP synthesis.', 'It measures DNA in a cell.'], why: 'Proteomics helps compare protein expression, modifications, and interactions under different conditions.', analogy: 'It is like cataloging every tool in a workshop and what each one does.' },
113:     { topic: 'the significance of amino acid chirality', correct: 'Most natural amino acids in proteins are L-amino acids, giving proteins a consistent stereochemical architecture.', wrongs: ['All amino acids are racemic and identical.', 'Only D-amino acids form proteins.', 'Chirality exists only in DNA.'], why: 'Chirality matters for enzyme recognition and the specific folding of proteins.', analogy: 'It is like a standard orientation that all parts are built to fit.' },
114:     { topic: 'the function of glycoproteins', correct: 'They are proteins covalently attached to carbohydrate groups and often participate in recognition or protection.', wrongs: ['They are only used for energy storage.', 'They consist solely of DNA.', 'They never leave the nucleus.'], why: 'Carbohydrate attachments often mediate recognition, adhesion, and immune interactions.', analogy: 'It is like attaching a name tag to a worker so others identify them correctly.' },
115:     { topic: 'the effect of phosphorylation on proteins', correct: 'It often alters charge and interactions, helping regulate enzyme activity and signaling.', wrongs: ['It always destroys the protein.', 'It only affects DNA sequence.', 'It makes all proteins fold into the same shape.'], why: 'Adding phosphate groups can switch proteins between active and inactive states.', analogy: 'It is like flipping a switch that changes how the machine runs.' },
116:     { topic: 'the source of protein diversity', correct: 'It arises mainly from the enormous variety of amino acid sequences and their interactions.', wrongs: ['It arises only from the number of cells in the body.', 'It comes from a fixed set of identical peptide bonds.', 'It arises only from DNA concentration.'], why: 'Different sequences build different structures, folds, and functions.', analogy: 'It is like using many different arrangements of the same blocks to build unique structures.' },
117:     { topic: 'the role of the protein backbone in hydrogen bonding', correct: 'It provides repeated carbonyl and amide groups that participate in stabilizing secondary structure.', wrongs: ['It has no role because only side chains form hydrogen bonds.', 'It uses phosphate groups for bonding.', 'It is never involved in folded structure.'], why: 'Backbone atoms form directional hydrogen bonds central to helices and sheets.', analogy: 'It is like a ladder whose rungs connect the rails in a repeating pattern.' },
118:     { topic: 'the significance of enzyme specificity', correct: 'It prevents a cell from wasting energy on inappropriate reactions and supports precise metabolism.', wrongs: ['It makes every enzyme do the same job.', 'It eliminates the need for regulation.', 'It is only relevant in DNA.'], why: 'A specific enzyme binds the right substrate and helps direct chemical pathways efficiently.', analogy: 'It is like a specialized tool for one task instead of a universal hammer for everything.' },
119:     { topic: 'the role of zinc in some enzymes', correct: 'It can stabilize a catalytic site or participate directly in electron transfer or acid-base chemistry.', wrongs: ['It only acts as a passive membrane component.', 'It replaces all amino acids in the active site.', 'It is purely structural and never catalytic.'], why: 'Metal cofactors can contribute Lewis acid character or coordinate reactants in certain enzyme mechanisms.', analogy: 'It is like a specialized clamp holding the workpiece in exactly the right place.' },

## Objective
- Expand the existing game into a complete, playable biochemistry learning game based on *Lehninger Principles of Biochemistry*.

## Requirements
- Add chapters covering amino acids (structure, polarity, special functions), three-dimensional protein structure, protein function, enzymes, carbohydrates, lipids, nucleotides, and nucleic acids.
- Add a chapter-specific word bank with definitions, viewable by holding a chapter in the menu.
- Add modes for explaining answers in the player’s own words, defining words in their own words, and studying all questions.
- Build now without asking clarifying questions; note reasonable assumptions when finished.

## Decisions
- (none)

## Work State
### Completed
- Inspected the existing game files and structure.

### Active
- Implement the requested chapters, word banks, and game modes.
- Run the app and relevant checks; capture and inspect the latest small JPEG screenshot.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Inspect the remaining portions of the existing game and implement the requested content and interactions.
2. Run the app and relevant checks; save and inspect the latest JPEG screenshot.
3. Summarize implementation, validation, and assumptions.

## Relevant Files
- `game.js`: Existing game content and gameplay logic.
- `bank-a.js`: Existing question bank.
- `index.html`: App structure.
- `styles.css`: App styling.
- `start.sh`, `startup.sh`, `capture.sh`: Existing run and capture scripts.

## Important Context
- No implementation or validation work has been reported yet.

3:     { q: 'What kind of bond links amino acids together in a protein?', answers: [

9:       ['The R group (side chain)', true, 'The R group is the variable side chain. Its chemistry—size, charge, polarity—gives each amino acid its personality and helps determine how proteins fold.'],
10:       ['The amino group', false, 'The amino group is shared by the standard amino acids. It is the side chain, or R group, that changes and makes each one distinct.'],

18:     { q: 'What does a buffer do when a small amount of acid is added?', answers: [

21:       ['It releases only hydroxide ions', false, 'A buffer is a paired system that can take up or donate protons depending on what is added. It does not simply release hydroxide.'],

109:     { topic: 'the importance of protein structure for function', correct: 'A protein’s function depends on its precise three-dimensional structure and the residues exposed to its environment.', wrongs: ['Function depends only on amino acid count.', 'Structure has no effect on the process it carries out.', 'Only DNA sequence matters for activity.'], why: 'The arrangement of side chains creates pockets, surfaces, and dynamic motions needed for function.', analogy: 'It is like a machine being useful only when every part is assembled in the right place.' },

111:     { topic: 'the contribution of peptide bonds to flexibility', correct: 'They are rigid enough to maintain the backbone, yet allow rotation in the surrounding bonds.', wrongs: ['They are completely rigid in every direction.', 'They allow free rotation around every atom.', 'They are only present in DNA.'], why: 'The partial double-bond character of the peptide bond restricts rotation, but neighboring bonds retain flexibility.', analogy: 'It is like a chain that keeps its order but still bends between links.' },
112:     { topic: 'the use of proteomics', correct: 'It studies the complete set of proteins and their functions in a cell or tissue.', wrongs: ['It studies only the lipid bilayer.', 'It studies only ATP synthesis.', 'It measures DNA in a cell.'], why: 'Proteomics helps compare protein expression, modifications, and interactions under different conditions.', analogy: 'It is like cataloging every tool in a workshop and what each one does.' },
113:     { topic: 'the significance of amino acid chirality', correct: 'Most natural amino acids in proteins are L-amino acids, giving proteins a consistent stereochemical architecture.', wrongs: ['All amino acids are racemic and identical.', 'Only D-amino acids form proteins.', 'Chirality exists only in DNA.'], why: 'Chirality matters for enzyme recognition and the specific folding of proteins.', analogy: 'It is like a standard orientation that all parts are built to fit.' },
114:     { topic: 'the function of glycoproteins', correct: 'They are proteins covalently attached to carbohydrate groups and often participate in recognition or protection.', wrongs: ['They are only used for energy storage.', 'They consist solely of DNA.', 'They never leave the nucleus.'], why: 'Carbohydrate attachments often mediate recognition, adhesion, and immune interactions.', analogy: 'It is like attaching a name tag to a worker so others identify them correctly.' },

116:     { topic: 'the source of protein diversity', correct: 'It arises mainly from the enormous variety of amino acid sequences and their interactions.', wrongs: ['It arises only from the number of cells in the body.', 'It comes from a fixed set of identical peptide bonds.', 'It arises only from DNA concentration.'], why: 'Different sequences build different structures, folds, and functions.', analogy: 'It is like using many different arrangements of the same blocks to build unique structures.' },
117:     { topic: 'the role of the protein backbone in hydrogen bonding', correct: 'It provides repeated carbonyl and amide groups that participate in stabilizing secondary structure.', wrongs: ['It has no role because only side chains form hydrogen bonds.', 'It uses phosphate groups for bonding.', 'It is never involved in folded structure.'], why: 'Backbone atoms form directional hydrogen bonds central to helices and sheets.', analogy: 'It is like a ladder whose rungs connect the rails in a repeating pattern.' },
118:     { topic: 'the significance of enzyme specificity', correct: 'It prevents a cell from wasting energy on inappropriate reactions and supports precise metabolism.', wrongs: ['It makes every enzyme do the same job.', 'It eliminates the need for regulation.', 'It is only relevant in DNA.'], why: 'A specific enzyme binds the right substrate and helps direct chemical pathways efficiently.', analogy: 'It is like a specialized tool for one task instead of a universal hammer for everything.' },

## Objective
- Expand the existing game into a complete, playable biochemistry learning game based on *Lehninger Principles of Biochemistry*.

## Requirements
- Add chapters covering amino acids (structure, polarity, special functions), three-dimensional protein structure, protein function, enzymes, carbohydrates, lipids, nucleotides, and nucleic acids.
- Add a chapter-specific word bank with definitions, viewable by holding a chapter in the menu.
- Add modes for explaining answers in the player’s own words, defining words in their own words, and studying all questions.
- Build and validate the app; note reasonable assumptions when finished.

## Decisions
- No additional decisions recorded.

## Work State
### Completed
- Inspected portions of `game.js`, `bank-a.js`, `index.html`, `styles.css`, and the startup/capture scripts.

### Active
- Implement requested chapters, word banks, and learning modes.
- Run the app and relevant checks; capture and inspect the latest small JPEG screenshot.

### Blocked
- None.

## Next Move
1. Inspect remaining game logic and implement the requested content and interactions.
2. Run the app and relevant checks; save and inspect the latest JPEG screenshot.
3. Summarize implementation, validation, and assumptions.

## Relevant Files
- `game.js`: Existing chapter content and gameplay logic.
- `bank-a.js`: Existing question bank.
- `index.html`: App structure.
- `styles.css`: App styling.
- `start.sh`, `startup.sh`, `capture.sh`: Run and capture scripts.

## Important Context
- No implementation or validation work has been reported yet.

23:     { topic: 'a condensation reaction', correct: 'It forms a larger molecule while releasing water.', wrongs: ['It consumes water to make a larger molecule.', 'It rearranges only metal ions.', 'It always makes ATP.'], why: 'Condensation joins two molecules by eliminating water, as seen in peptide and glycosidic bond formation.', analogy: 'It is like assembling bricks and dropping the excess mortar away.' },
24:     { topic: 'a free-energy change (ΔG)', correct: 'It predicts whether a process is favorable under the given conditions.', wrongs: ['It tells the exact speed of a reaction.', 'It is always positive for every biological process.', 'It is the same as pH.'], why: 'Thermodynamics describes spontaneity; kinetics describes rate, and those are separate concepts.', analogy: 'It is like knowing whether a hill is downhill without saying how fast you will roll.' },
25:     { topic: 'the role of hydrogen bonds in proteins', correct: 'They help stabilize local structures and influence folding and specificity.', wrongs: ['They are the covalent links that form the backbone.', 'They create ATP directly.', 'They are the same as peptide bonds.'], why: 'Hydrogen bonds are key interactions among backbone atoms and side chains, but they do not replace the covalent chain itself.', analogy: 'They are like the handrails that keep a staircase stable without being the steps.' },
26:     { topic: 'the linkage in a nucleic acid backbone', correct: 'It is a phosphodiester bond connecting the sugar-phosphate chain.', wrongs: ['It is a peptide bond between nitrogen bases.', 'It is a hydrogen bond between phosphate groups.', 'It is a glycosidic bond only in proteins.'], why: 'Phosphodiester bonds join nucleotides into DNA and RNA polymers, forming the sugar-phosphate backbone.', analogy: 'It is like the metal bars linking a series of small platforms.' },
27:     { topic: 'the most important property of an enzyme’s substrate-binding site', correct: 'It is specific enough to bind the correct substrate and orient it for catalysis.', wrongs: ['It binds every molecule in the cell equally well.', 'It stores genetic information.', 'It increases the number of moles of a reaction.'], why: 'Specific binding promotes productive interactions and reduces wasteful side reactions.', analogy: 'It is like a lock and key that fits only the correct shape and aligns it for turning.' },
28:     { topic: 'the difference between a weak acid and a strong acid', correct: 'A weak acid partially dissociates, while a strong acid dissociates nearly completely.', wrongs: ['A weak acid has no protons to donate.', 'A strong acid is always basic.', 'Only weak acids are found in cells.'], why: 'Strength depends on how readily the acid transfers protons in water, not simply on how much acid is present.', analogy: 'It is like two workers: one gives away most of what they carry, while the other gives only part of it.' },
29:     { topic: 'the use of oxidation states in metabolism', correct: 'They track electron loss and gain and help identify redox reactions.', wrongs: ['They describe only pH.', 'They measure temperature in the cell.', 'They show the number of hydrogen bonds.'], why: 'Oxidation and reduction involve electron transfer, and oxidation states make these changes easier to follow.', analogy: 'It is like keeping score in a game where electrons are the points being exchanged.' },
30:     { topic: 'the role of chiral centers in amino acids', correct: 'They make amino acids stereoisomers, usually with L configuration in proteins.', wrongs: ['They eliminate all protein folding.', 'They make every amino acid identical.', 'They are only found in fatty acids.'], why: 'The tetrahedral arrangement around the alpha carbon creates asymmetry, and biological systems often use one stereochemical form.', analogy: 'It is like a hand with a left- and right-handed grip; the cell uses one orientation consistently.' },

33:     { topic: 'the main reason proteins fold into stable shapes', correct: 'They minimize free energy by balancing covalent, electrostatic, hydrogen-bond, van der Waals, and hydrophobic interactions.', wrongs: ['They fold only because of ATP hydrolysis.', 'They form random shapes without any rules.', 'They fold only in the nucleus.'], why: 'Protein folding is driven by physical interactions that favor one low-energy conformation over many alternatives.', analogy: 'It is like arranging furniture to fit a room and keep it stable without crowding it.' },

window.extraLearningChapters = [
  {
    id: 'amino-acids', name: 'Amino Acids', short: 'AMINO ACIDS', subtitle: 'Structure, polarity & special roles', icon: '⌁', topic: 'AMINO ACID CHEMISTRY',
    words: [
      ['alpha carbon', 'The central carbon in a standard amino acid, bonded to an amino group, a carboxyl group, hydrogen, and a side chain.'],
      ['amino group', 'The nitrogen-containing group; in proteins it is part of the shared amino-acid backbone.'],
      ['carboxyl group', 'The acidic carbon-containing group that is part of every standard amino-acid backbone.'],
      ['R group', 'The variable side chain that gives each amino acid its characteristic size and chemistry.'],
      ['zwitterion', 'A molecule bearing both positive and negative charges while having no net charge overall.'],
      ['isoelectric point (pI)', 'The pH at which a molecule has zero average net electrical charge.'],
      ['essential amino acid', 'An amino acid that an organism cannot synthesize in sufficient amount and must obtain from its diet.'],
      ['hydrophobic', 'Describes a nonpolar group that interacts poorly with water and tends to associate with other nonpolar surfaces.'],
      ['polar', 'Describes a group with an uneven distribution of electrical charge that can interact favorably with water.'],
      ['disulfide bond', 'A covalent bond between the sulfur atoms of two cysteine side chains, helping stabilize some protein structures.'],
      ['proline', 'An amino acid whose cyclic side chain constrains its backbone and can introduce a bend or disrupt an alpha helix.'],
      ['glycine', 'The smallest amino acid, with hydrogen as its side chain; its small size allows unusual backbone flexibility.']
    ],
    questions: [
      { q: 'Which groups are attached to the alpha carbon of a typical amino acid?', answers: [
        ['An amino group, carboxyl group, hydrogen, and R group', true, 'These four substituents define the common amino-acid structure. The R group varies and determines much of each amino acid’s chemistry.'],
        ['A phosphate, two sugars, and a base', false, 'Those components describe a nucleotide, not an amino acid. The amino acid has an amino group, carboxyl group, hydrogen, and side chain.'],
        ['Three fatty-acid tails and glycerol', false, 'That is closer to a lipid structure. Amino acids share a central alpha carbon with four attached groups.'],
        ['Four identical R groups', false, 'The four groups are not identical: they include amino, carboxyl, hydrogen, and a variable R group.']] },
      { q: 'At physiological pH, many free amino acids exist mainly as…', answers: [
        ['Zwitterions, with a positive amino group and negative carboxyl group', true, 'Near physiological pH, the amino group is commonly protonated and the carboxyl group deprotonated. Both charges are present, although their sum can be zero.'],
        ['Uncharged molecules with no ionic groups', false, 'Amino acids commonly carry ionized amino and carboxyl groups in water; zero net charge does not mean no charges.'],
        ['A pair of covalently joined amino acids', false, 'A pair joined by a peptide bond is a dipeptide. A free amino acid is not necessarily joined to another.'],
        ['Negatively charged only at every pH', false, 'The net charge depends on pH and ionizable groups. Near physiological pH many amino acids have both positive and negative charges.']] },
      { q: 'Which side chain is most likely to be found in a water-exposed, polar region?', answers: [
        ['Serine, whose side chain contains a hydroxyl group', true, 'Serine’s hydroxyl group is polar and can form hydrogen bonds with water and other groups.'],
        ['Leucine, with a largely hydrocarbon side chain', false, 'Leucine is nonpolar and hydrophobic, so it often packs into a protein interior rather than favoring water.'],
        ['Phenylalanine, with a nonpolar aromatic ring', false, 'Its aromatic side chain is largely hydrophobic, unlike serine’s polar hydroxyl.'],
        ['Isoleucine, with a branched hydrocarbon side chain', false, 'Isoleucine is nonpolar and generally avoids direct contact with water.']] },
      { q: 'Why can glycine fit into tight turns in some proteins?', answers: [
        ['Its side chain is only a hydrogen, giving it unusual backbone flexibility', true, 'Glycine has the smallest side chain, so it is less sterically restricted and can adopt backbone angles that many other residues cannot.'],
        ['Its side chain forms a permanent disulfide bond', false, 'Cysteine, not glycine, has a sulfur-containing side chain that can form disulfide bonds.'],
        ['It has no alpha carbon', false, 'Glycine has the standard alpha carbon; only its side chain is especially small.'],
        ['It is always positively charged', false, 'Glycine’s side chain is not charged. Its flexibility comes from its minimal size.']] },
      { q: 'What special structural effect can proline have in a polypeptide?', answers: [

        ['It creates a peptide bond without a backbone', false, 'Proline is incorporated into the ordinary polypeptide backbone; it does not eliminate the backbone.'],
        ['It always forms a disulfide cross-link', false, 'Disulfide bonds form between cysteine side chains, not proline.'],
        ['It makes every protein soluble in oil', false, 'Amino-acid composition can influence solubility, but proline does not make every protein oil-soluble.']] }

  {

      ['primary structure', 'The linear amino-acid sequence of a polypeptide, including the positions of covalent cross-links when specified.'],

      ['alpha helix', 'A common helical secondary structure stabilized by hydrogen bonds between backbone groups.'],
      ['beta sheet', 'A secondary structure formed by aligned beta strands connected by backbone hydrogen bonds.'],
      ['tertiary structure', 'The overall three-dimensional arrangement of a single polypeptide chain.'],
      ['quaternary structure', 'The arrangement and interactions of multiple polypeptide subunits in a protein assembly.'],
      ['hydrophobic effect', 'The tendency of nonpolar surfaces to cluster in water, often driving nonpolar residues toward a protein core.'],
      ['denaturation', 'Disruption of a protein’s native higher-order structure, commonly impairing function without necessarily breaking peptide bonds.'],
      ['disulfide bond', 'A covalent link between two cysteine side chains that can stabilize a folded protein.'],
      ['conformation', 'A particular three-dimensional shape accessible to a molecule through rotations and structural rearrangements.'],

    questions: [
      { q: 'Which interactions directly stabilize an alpha helix and beta sheet?', answers: [

        ['Peptide bonds between separate side chains', false, 'Peptide bonds connect successive amino acids in the chain; they are not the repeating stabilizing interactions between helix or sheet segments.'],
        ['Phosphodiester bonds between residues', false, 'Phosphodiester bonds connect nucleotides in nucleic acids, not protein secondary structures.'],
        ['Disulfide bonds at every turn', false, 'Disulfides can stabilize some proteins, but alpha helices and beta sheets are principally stabilized by backbone hydrogen bonds.']] },
      { q: 'What best describes tertiary structure?', answers: [
        ['The overall three-dimensional fold of one polypeptide chain', true, 'Tertiary structure describes how the full chain, including its secondary structures, packs into a three-dimensional form.'],
        ['The amino-acid sequence alone', false, 'The sequence is primary structure. Tertiary structure is the chain’s overall 3D fold.'],
        ['The arrangement of DNA bases in a chromosome', false, 'That concerns nucleic-acid organization, not a protein’s tertiary structure.'],
        ['Only the local hydrogen bonds of one alpha helix', false, 'An alpha helix is secondary structure; tertiary structure describes the overall fold.']] },
      { q: 'A protein has four associated polypeptide chains. Which structural level describes their assembly?', answers: [

        ['Primary structure', false, 'Primary structure is the amino-acid sequence of an individual chain.'],
        ['Secondary structure', false, 'Secondary structure refers to local alpha helices and beta sheets.'],
        ['Tertiary structure only', false, 'Tertiary structure describes a single chain’s fold; the arrangement among several chains is quaternary structure.']] },
      { q: 'Why do many soluble proteins bury hydrophobic side chains in their interior?', answers: [
        ['Packing them away from water can lower the system’s free energy', true, 'Exposing nonpolar surfaces disrupts water’s hydrogen-bonding network. Burial of hydrophobic groups is a major contributor to folding, alongside other interactions.'],
        ['The protein interior is always full of oil', false, 'Protein interiors are not oil-filled; hydrophobic residues pack together in a protein environment.'],
        ['Hydrophobic side chains make peptide bonds stronger', false, 'Peptide bonds link the backbone. Hydrophobic packing contributes to folding but does not strengthen those covalent bonds.'],
        ['Water cannot enter any folded protein', false, 'Some water may be present in protein interiors and cavities. Folding reduces unfavorable exposure rather than excluding every water molecule.']] },
      { q: 'What is a likely effect of heat or extreme pH on a protein?', answers: [

    questions: [

        ['Denaturation', false, 'Denaturation is loss of native structure, not the specific, often reversible shape adjustment associated with ligand binding.']] },

        ['It permanently replaces the protein’s amino-acid sequence', false, 'Allosteric effectors bind noncovalently or covalently in regulatory ways; they do not rewrite the protein sequence.'],

        ['It only works by changing the DNA code', false, 'Allostery is direct regulation through protein structure and interactions, not necessarily through DNA.']] },
      { q: 'What does cooperative oxygen binding mean for hemoglobin?', answers: [

      { q: 'Which statement distinguishes myoglobin from hemoglobin?', answers: [

      { q: 'A motor protein’s core job is to…', answers: [

  {

    questions: [

        ['It changes the equilibrium constant', false, 'A catalyst speeds both forward and reverse reactions and does not change equilibrium.'],
        ['It is consumed to become part of the product', false, 'Enzymes are regenerated at the end of catalytic cycles, although they can eventually be degraded or inactivated.']] },
      { q: 'What is the enzyme’s active site?', answers: [

  {

      ['monosaccharide', 'A single sugar unit that cannot be hydrolyzed into a simpler carbohydrate.'],

## Objective
- Expand the existing game into a complete, playable biochemistry learning game based on *Lehninger Principles of Biochemistry*.

## Requirements
- Add chapters covering amino acids, three-dimensional protein structure, protein function, enzymes, carbohydrates, lipids, nucleotides, and nucleic acids.
- Add a chapter-specific word bank with definitions, viewable by holding a chapter in the menu.
- Add modes for explaining answers in the player’s own words, defining words in their own words, and studying all questions.
- Build and validate the app; note reasonable assumptions when finished.

## Decisions
- (none)

### Completed
- Inspected portions of `game.js`, `bank-a.js`, and `index.html`; checked repository files and status.

### Active
- Implement requested chapters, word banks, and learning modes.
- Run the app and relevant checks; capture and inspect the latest small JPEG screenshot.

### Blocked
- (none)

1. Inspect remaining game logic and implement the requested content and interactions.
2. Run the app and relevant checks; save and inspect the latest JPEG screenshot.
3. Summarize implementation, validation, and assumptions.

- `bank-a.js`: Existing question bank.
- `index.html`: App structure.
- `styles.css`: App styling.
- `start.sh`, `startup.sh`, `capture.sh`: Run and capture scripts.

## Important Context
- No implementation or validation work has been reported yet.

91:     { topic: 'the tertiary structure of a protein', correct: 'It is the overall three-dimensional shape of a single polypeptide chain.', wrongs: ['It is just the amino acid sequence.', 'It is the arrangement of membranes around the protein.', 'It is always identical for all proteins.'], why: 'Tertiary structure includes folding, loops, and interactions across the entire chain.', analogy: 'It is like the final sculpted form of a clay figure.' },
92:     { topic: 'quaternary structure', correct: 'It is the assembly of multiple polypeptide subunits into one functional protein.', wrongs: ['It is the same as the peptide bond.', 'It is present in a single free amino acid.', 'It is only found in DNA.'], why: 'Some proteins are composed of several chains whose interaction creates active function.', analogy: 'It is like a team of workers combining to operate a machine.' },
93:     { topic: 'a denatured protein', correct: 'It has lost its native structure and often its function, though the sequence remains intact.', wrongs: ['It has broken into smaller amino acids only.', 'It always gains a new active site.', 'It is only denatured in the ribosome.'], why: 'Denaturation disrupts noncovalent interactions that maintain folding, but the covalent backbone remains.', analogy: 'It is like a folded paper being crumpled but not shredded into pieces.' },
94:     { topic: 'a competitive inhibitor', correct: 'It binds the active site and competes directly with the substrate.', wrongs: ['It binds a distant site and never blocks binding.', 'It breaks peptide bonds.', 'It turns the enzyme into a membrane.'], why: 'Competitive inhibition lowers substrate access to the active site and can be overcome by more substrate.', analogy: 'It is like a person blocking the entrance to a room while waiting for a customer.' },
95:     { topic: 'a noncompetitive inhibitor', correct: 'It binds elsewhere and can reduce enzyme activity without directly competing for the active site.', wrongs: ['It only binds the substrate itself.', 'It always increases the enzyme’s affinity for substrate.', 'It is the same as a peptide bond.'], why: 'Binding away from the active site can alter conformation and reduce catalysis.', analogy: 'It is like loosening the steering wheel rather than standing in the doorway.' },
96:     { topic: 'the role of metal ions in proteins', correct: 'They can stabilize structures or participate directly in catalysis as cofactors.', wrongs: ['They are always the same as amino acids.', 'They only appear in DNA.', 'They remove the need for folding.'], why: 'Metal ions can coordinate ligands, mediate electron transfer, or assist in enzyme chemistry.', analogy: 'They are like specialized tools in a workshop that help handle difficult jobs.' },
97:     { topic: 'a prosthetic group', correct: 'It is a tightly bound non-polypeptide component required for some proteins to function.', wrongs: ['It is a free amino acid that is never bound.', 'It is the same as a peptide bond.', 'It is only found in membranes.'], why: 'Prosthetic groups like heme or biotin help define function and may be required for catalysis or binding.', analogy: 'It is like a permanent accessory attached to a machine to let it do its job.' },
98:     { topic: 'the reason proteins often require chaperones', correct: 'They help prevent aggregation and assist folding in crowded cellular environments.', wrongs: ['They are only involved in DNA replication.', 'They make proteins spontaneously fold without any information.', 'They remove all hydrophobic interactions.'], why: 'The cell is crowded, and misfolding can be costly, so chaperones assist in productive folding.', analogy: 'They are like guides helping a traveler through a crowded and confusing city.' },
99:     { topic: 'the role of hydrophobic residues in folding', correct: 'They tend to pack into the core of the protein to minimize contact with water.', wrongs: ['They always remain on the surface.', 'They prevent all hydrogen bonding.', 'They are irrelevant to stability.'], why: 'Hydrophobic collapse reduces unfavorable water ordering and contributes strongly to stabilizing the folded form.', analogy: 'It is like placing the rain-sensitive parts inside a shelter to protect them.' },
100:     { topic: 'the difference between an enzyme and a protein', correct: 'All enzymes are proteins, but not all proteins are enzymes.', wrongs: ['All proteins are enzymes.', 'Only ribosomes are enzymes.', 'Proteins do not participate in catalysis.'], why: 'Enzymes are catalytic proteins, while many proteins serve structural, transport, signaling, or storage roles.', analogy: 'It is like all squares being rectangles, but not all rectangles being squares.' },
101:     { topic: 'the role of hydrogen bonds in alpha helices', correct: 'They form between the carbonyl oxygen and amide hydrogen of nearby residues along the backbone.', wrongs: ['They connect side chains only at random points.', 'They form between DNA bases only.', 'They make peptide bonds.'], why: 'Regular hydrogen-bonding patterns stabilize helical geometry and maintain secondary structure.', analogy: 'It is like repeated handholds holding a climber in a stable pattern.' },
102:     { topic: 'the meaning of a protein’s ligand', correct: 'It is a molecule that binds specifically to the protein and can modulate its function.', wrongs: ['It is the same as the peptide backbone.', 'It is the product after catalysis.', 'It is always a large membrane lipid.'], why: 'Ligands can activate, inhibit, stabilize, or deliver signals to proteins.', analogy: 'It is like a key that fits a lock and turns it to change the action.' },
103:     { topic: 'the role of disulfide bonds', correct: 'They are covalent cross-links that can stabilize protein structure, especially extracellular proteins.', wrongs: ['They are the main bonds in the protein backbone.', 'They are always temporary and weak.', 'They only appear in DNA.'], why: 'Cysteine side chains can form covalent disulfide bridges that reinforce folding.', analogy: 'They are like sturdy braces holding a frame together.' },
104:     { topic: 'the post-translational modification of a protein', correct: 'It is a covalent chemical change made after translation that can regulate activity or targeting.', wrongs: ['It occurs only in DNA before translation.', 'It is the same as amino acid polymerization.', 'It always destroys the protein.'], why: 'Modifications like phosphorylation or glycosylation affect structure, localization, and signaling.', analogy: 'It is like adding decals or upgrades to a finished machine.' },
105:     { topic: 'the importance of protein folding in disease', correct: 'Misfolding can expose hydrophobic surfaces or trap proteins in nonfunctional states and contribute to disease.', wrongs: ['Protein folding never changes biological function.', 'Diseases only come from DNA mutations.', 'Misfolding is always harmless.'], why: 'Misfolded proteins can aggregate or fail to bind their correct partners, disrupting normal cell processes.', analogy: 'It is like a desk organizer being thrown into a pile and no longer usable.' },
106:     { topic: 'the significance of side-chain charge in protein function', correct: 'Charged side chains can participate in ionic interactions, catalysis, and binding specificity.', wrongs: ['Charge never matters because the backbone controls everything.', 'Only hydrophobic groups create function.', 'Charge only matters in water but not inside proteins.'], why: 'Electrostatic interactions help define structure and are often essential for enzyme active sites.', analogy: 'It is like the combination of different colored wires powering different components.' },
107:     { topic: 'the meaning of protein specificity', correct: 'It is the ability of a protein to preferentially bind or act on one set of molecules among many.', wrongs: ['It means the protein works on all molecules equally.', 'It is only about thermal stability.', 'It refers to DNA sequence alone.'], why: 'Specificity arises from geometric and chemical complementarity between the protein and its target.', analogy: 'It is like a tailored glove that fits one hand better than all others.' },
108:     { topic: 'the role of the active site in catalysis', correct: 'It arranges substrates and catalytic groups to lower the activation barrier.', wrongs: ['It makes the reaction irreversible by itself.', 'It is the region that stores genetic information.', 'It is a passive storage pocket with no chemistry.'], why: 'Enzyme active sites create an environment that stabilizes the transition state and orients reacting groups.', analogy: 'It is like a workshop bench where tools are positioned for efficient work.' },
109:     { topic: 'the importance of protein structure for function', correct: 'A protein’s function depends on its precise three-dimensional structure and the residues exposed to its environment.', wrongs: ['Function depends only on amino acid count.', 'Structure has no effect on the process it carries out.', 'Only DNA sequence matters for activity.'], why: 'The arrangement of side chains creates pockets, surfaces, and dynamic motions needed for function.', analogy: 'It is like a machine being useful only when every part is assembled in the right place.' },
110:     { topic: 'translation in protein synthesis', correct: 'It is the process by which ribosomes read mRNA and assemble amino acids into a polypeptide.', wrongs: ['It copies DNA into RNA.', 'It forms phospholipids from amino acids.', 'It is a form of denaturation.'], why: 'Translation converts the genetic code into a protein with a defined sequence.', analogy: 'It is like using a blueprint to build a structure one piece at a time.' },
111:     { topic: 'the contribution of peptide bonds to flexibility', correct: 'They are rigid enough to maintain the backbone, yet allow rotation in the surrounding bonds.', wrongs: ['They are completely rigid in every direction.', 'They allow free rotation around every atom.', 'They are only present in DNA.'], why: 'The partial double-bond character of the peptide bond restricts rotation, but neighboring bonds retain flexibility.', analogy: 'It is like a chain that keeps its order but still bends between links.' },
112:     { topic: 'the use of proteomics', correct: 'It studies the complete set of proteins and their functions in a cell or tissue.', wrongs: ['It studies only the lipid bilayer.', 'It studies only ATP synthesis.', 'It measures DNA in a cell.'], why: 'Proteomics helps compare protein expression, modifications, and interactions under different conditions.', analogy: 'It is like cataloging every tool in a workshop and what each one does.' },
113:     { topic: 'the significance of amino acid chirality', correct: 'Most natural amino acids in proteins are L-amino acids, giving proteins a consistent stereochemical architecture.', wrongs: ['All amino acids are racemic and identical.', 'Only D-amino acids form proteins.', 'Chirality exists only in DNA.'], why: 'Chirality matters for enzyme recognition and the specific folding of proteins.', analogy: 'It is like a standard orientation that all parts are built to fit.' },
114:     { topic: 'the function of glycoproteins', correct: 'They are proteins covalently attached to carbohydrate groups and often participate in recognition or protection.', wrongs: ['They are only used for energy storage.', 'They consist solely of DNA.', 'They never leave the nucleus.'], why: 'Carbohydrate attachments often mediate recognition, adhesion, and immune interactions.', analogy: 'It is like attaching a name tag to a worker so others identify them correctly.' },
115:     { topic: 'the effect of phosphorylation on proteins', correct: 'It often alters charge and interactions, helping regulate enzyme activity and signaling.', wrongs: ['It always destroys the protein.', 'It only affects DNA sequence.', 'It makes all proteins fold into the same shape.'], why: 'Adding phosphate groups can switch proteins between active and inactive states.', analogy: 'It is like flipping a switch that changes how the machine runs.' },
116:     { topic: 'the source of protein diversity', correct: 'It arises mainly from the enormous variety of amino acid sequences and their interactions.', wrongs: ['It arises only from the number of cells in the body.', 'It comes from a fixed set of identical peptide bonds.', 'It arises only from DNA concentration.'], why: 'Different sequences build different structures, folds, and functions.', analogy: 'It is like using many different arrangements of the same blocks to build unique structures.' },
117:     { topic: 'the role of the protein backbone in hydrogen bonding', correct: 'It provides repeated carbonyl and amide groups that participate in stabilizing secondary structure.', wrongs: ['It has no role because only side chains form hydrogen bonds.', 'It uses phosphate groups for bonding.', 'It is never involved in folded structure.'], why: 'Backbone atoms form directional hydrogen bonds central to helices and sheets.', analogy: 'It is like a ladder whose rungs connect the rails in a repeating pattern.' },
118:     { topic: 'the significance of enzyme specificity', correct: 'It prevents a cell from wasting energy on inappropriate reactions and supports precise metabolism.', wrongs: ['It makes every enzyme do the same job.', 'It eliminates the need for regulation.', 'It is only relevant in DNA.'], why: 'A specific enzyme binds the right substrate and helps direct chemical pathways efficiently.', analogy: 'It is like a specialized tool for one task instead of a universal hammer for everything.' },
119:     { topic: 'the role of zinc in some enzymes', correct: 'It can stabilize a catalytic site or participate directly in electron transfer or acid-base chemistry.', wrongs: ['It only acts as a passive membrane component.', 'It replaces all amino acids in the active site.', 'It is purely structural and never catalytic.'], why: 'Metal cofactors can contribute Lewis acid character or coordinate reactants in certain enzyme mechanisms.', analogy: 'It is like a specialized clamp holding the workpiece in exactly the right place.' },

messages.summary:
## Objective
- Expand the existing game into a complete, playable biochemistry learning game based on *Lehninger Principles of Biochemistry*.

## Requirements
- Add chapters for amino acids, three-dimensional protein structure, protein function, enzymes, carbohydrates, lipids, nucleotides, and nucleic acids.
- Provide chapter-specific word banks with definitions, viewable by holding a chapter in the menu.
- Add modes for explaining answers in the player’s own words, defining words in their own words, and studying all questions.
- Build and validate the app, capture and inspect the latest small JPEG screenshot, and note reasonable assumptions when finished.

## Decisions
- No additional decisions recorded.

## Work State
### Completed
- Inspected portions of `game.js`, `bank-a.js`, `index.html`, `styles.css`, and project scripts.
- Created `learning-data.js` with eight requested chapter entries, each containing word definitions and five multiple-choice questions.

### Active
- Integrate the chapter data with the existing game and implement the requested word-bank interaction and learning modes.
- Run the app and relevant checks; capture and inspect the latest small JPEG screenshot.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Inspect the remaining gameplay logic in `game.js`, `index.html`, and `styles.css`; integrate `learning-data.js` and implement the requested interactions.
2. Run the app and checks, capture and inspect the latest small JPEG screenshot.
3. Summarize implementation, validation, and assumptions.

## Relevant Files
- `learning-data.js`: New chapter questions and word-bank definitions.
- `game.js`: Existing chapter content and gameplay logic to integrate with.
- `bank-a.js`: Existing question-bank structure and content.
- `index.html`: App structure and script loading.
- `styles.css`: App styling.
- `start.sh`, `startup.sh`, `capture.sh`: Run and capture scripts.

## Important Context
- `learning-data.js` currently assigns data to `window.extraLearningChapters`; it has not yet been integrated into the app.
- Implementation and validation are incomplete.

3:     { q: 'What kind of bond links amino acids together in a protein?', answers: [
4:       ['A peptide bond', true, 'A peptide bond forms between the amino group of one amino acid and the carboxyl group of another, joining them into a chain. Think of it as the sturdy link in a molecular necklace.'],
5:       ['A hydrogen bond', false, 'Hydrogen bonds help stabilize protein shapes, but they do not join amino acids into the chain itself. The chain is held together by peptide bonds.'],

8:     { q: 'Which part of an amino acid varies from one amino acid to another?', answers: [
9:       ['The R group (side chain)', true, 'The R group is the variable side chain. Its chemistry—size, charge, polarity—gives each amino acid its personality and helps determine how proteins fold.'],
10:       ['The amino group', false, 'The amino group is shared by the standard amino acids. It is the side chain, or R group, that changes and makes each one distinct.'],
11:       ['The alpha carbon', false, 'The alpha carbon is the central carbon shared by standard amino acids. The attached R group is the part that varies.'],

21:       ['It releases only hydroxide ions', false, 'A buffer is a paired system that can take up or donate protons depending on what is added. It does not simply release hydroxide.'],

36:       ['100 times', true, 'The pH scale is logarithmic. A two-unit drop means 10², or 100 times, more hydrogen ion concentration.'],
37:       ['2 times', false, 'Each pH unit is a tenfold change, not a onefold step. Two pH units mean 10 × 10 = 100 times.'],
38:       ['10 times', false, 'A one-unit difference is tenfold. From pH 5 to pH 3 is two units, so the difference is 100-fold.'],
39:       ['1,000 times', false, 'A three-unit difference would be 1,000-fold. Here the difference is two units: 100-fold.']] },
40:     { q: 'Which water property helps sweat cool your skin as it evaporates?', answers: [

42:       ['Low surface tension', false, 'Surface tension explains the “skin” at water’s surface, not the cooling effect of evaporation. Cooling comes from water’s high heat of vaporization.'],

44:       ['Its nonpolar nature', false, 'Water is polar. Its strong attractions take energy to overcome during evaporation, which is why sweat can cool you.']] },
45:     { q: 'In water, a hydrophobic molecule tends to…', answers: [
